text.p: Australian telecommunications manufacturer, Scitec Ltd was confident of reporting stronger second half earnings after posting a first half turnaround, the managing director, Paul Magee told Reuters on Thursday.
"The history of Scitec is always to have a much stronger second half than first half - there are a number of seasonal factors in there," Magee said in a telephone interview.

Scitec, the largest Australian-owned exporter of telecommunications equipment, earlier said its first half net earnings rose to A$302,000 from a loss of A$2.49 million in the previous corresponding half.
The company's flagship "Fastlane" range of products combine voice, data, fax and LAN (local area network) communications traffic onto one telephone line.
Scitec also manufactures frame relay access devices, network access equipment and is currently researching a range of products specifically for the ATM (Automated Teller Machine) access market.
Magee said the Scitec's return to profitability resulted from a refocus on existing products and markets to ensure sales were grown on a profitable basis.
"The gigantic turnaround really has come from living within our means. We have taken quite a lot of the expenses out of the business while still continuing to grow sales profitably," he said.
Magee said Scitec was encouraged by the continued strong sales growth of its products in Europe and Asia and said the company was confident this growth would continue.
"We spent a lot of time, effort and money in establishing those distribution channels over the last few years and now we are starting to reap some of the benefits," he said
Part of the company's success in Asia was due to its alliance with U.K.-based integrated network and telecommunications group, Case, which was formerly a part of the Cray Communications group.
"With Case, we have done over a A$1 million (of sales) into Korea over the last half year and we expect a lot more activity to come through there," Scitec finance manager, Dwin Tucker said.

Magee said Scitec was in the process of changing its organisational culture to reduce unnecessary overheads without affecting its research and development drive and its ability to successfully market products internationally.
"What we focused on in the past past was being much bigger and much quicker than we were. We were spending like a A$200 million company when we were only a A$50 million company," Magee said.
Scitec shares closed half a cent weaker at 22.5 cents.
